steps.heading: Hand it the frame, name the columns
steps.body: Seaborn sits on top of matplotlib and takes a different deal: give it the whole DataFrame once as data=, then refer to columns by name as strings. That is why x='region' works where pandas would need df['region'] — and it is what lets you name another column for hue or faceting without reshaping anything.

steps.heading: One call, one chart
steps.caption: Seaborn aggregates for you. Watch the default though: barplot shows the mean, not the sum, and draws a confidence interval on every bar unless you pass errorbar=None.

steps.heading: hue= is the whole trick
steps.body: Nearly every seaborn function takes hue=. Name a second categorical column and it splits the plot into one colour per value and builds the legend. The same keyword works on bars, scatters, lines and boxes — learn it once and it pays off everywhere.

steps.heading: A second dimension, for free
steps.code: sns.barplot(data=df, x='region', y='revenue', hue='category', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
steps.caption: No pivot, no reshaping. The long, raw frame was already the right shape.

steps.heading: The plots pandas doesn't have
steps.body: This is the real reason to reach for seaborn. Box plots and violins show how a group is spread out, not just its average. Heatmaps colour a whole pivoted table. regplot fits a trend line and shows how confident it is. Each is one line here and a small project in raw matplotlib.

steps.heading: Spread, not just average
steps.caption: The rule is the median, the box holds the middle half of the data, and the whiskers reach the rest. A bar chart would have collapsed each of these to a single number.

steps.heading: A whole table at a glance
steps.caption: heatmap can't reshape — it colours the table you hand it, so the pivot does the real work. annot=True writes the numbers in, which is what keeps it readable.

steps.heading: When hue runs out, facet
steps.body: Past a handful of groups, colour stops working — nobody can read a twelve-item legend. The figure-level functions (catplot, relplot, displot) take col= and draw one small panel per value instead. They share a scale across panels, which is what makes them comparable; that shared scale is the point, not a detail.

steps.heading: One panel per group
steps.code: sns.catplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', col='region', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
steps.caption: Only the figure-level functions can facet — barplot and boxplot cannot. Notice North's bars really are short: every panel is measured against the same axis.
